messages.author: 712207b40d408846
messages.subject: latent variable definition
parts:
Hi lavaan community,

I am wondering if there is the minimum number of observed variables to define a latent variable. Is it acceptable in lavaan to use two observed variables to define a latent variable or do we need to have at least three variables (or more) to define a latent variable? (I couldn't find this part from the tutorial or this group.)

Is it possible in lavaan to use an observed variable with a different Likert scale and from a different reporter with other observed variables? My two predictor observed variables are from the same reporter (child) about their mother and father (parenting) - exactly same items and same Likert (5-point), describing just mother or father. I also have observer's reports about mother (deals with the same parenting style), but with different items and a different Likert scale (9-point). In this case, can I use the observers' reports about mother with children's reports about mother and father to define a latent variable about parents' parenting style? If I so, do I need to do anything (e.g. convert 9-point to 5-point) to use it as the third observed variable with the other two?

I am assuming more observed variables are better to define a latent variable more correctly. Correct?

Thanks in advance,
NewInMediation

messages.author: 71bfb5f1e96782a8
messages.subject: Re: latent variable definition
parts:
Hi,

you need 3 observed variables to define a latent one. If i remember correctly, it is possible to define a latent variable by only two observed, but then you would need some other information on that latent variable (e.g. a covariance). 

From the technical side you can put any variables into the model as you like (e.g. different number of categories or from different observers). The point with the observers is that probably you are measuring two distinct constructs (e.g. the observers impression vs. the childs impression of the parenting style). Mixing them into one variable might not be appropriate.

More observed --> better definition: correct (when those observed variables measure the same variable, though). 

hth, felix
